topics.heading: Pipeline Gas Supply
bullets: Hospital pipeline systems supply medical gases at ~50–55 psi (the primary source during normal operation).
Pipeline gases include oxygen (O2), nitrous oxide (N2O), air, and nitrogen.
The Diameter Index Safety System (DISS) is a standardized, non-interchangeable threaded connector that prevents misconnection of different gas hoses at the anesthesia machine.

topics.heading: E-Cylinder Gas Supply
bullets: E-cylinders are the backup gas supply mounted on the anesthesia machine yoke.
The Pin Index Safety System (PISS) prevents attachment of the wrong cylinder to the wrong yoke — each gas has a unique pin configuration.
⚡ KEY: Oxygen is stored as COMPRESSED GAS — pressure is directly proportional to remaining volume. A half-full O2 E-cylinder reads ~1100 psi.
⚡ KEY: Nitrous oxide is stored as a LIQUID — pressure remains constant at ~745 psi until all liquid is vaporized. You CANNOT estimate remaining N2O by pressure alone; you must WEIGH the cylinder.
Duration formula: O2 Duration (min) = [Pressure (psi) × 0.3] ÷ Flow rate (L/min). Example: 1000 psi at 5 L/min → 60 minutes.

topics.heading: Fail-Safe System & Low-Pressure Alarms
bullets: The fail-safe system (pressure sensor shut-off valve) monitors O2 supply pressure.
If O2 pressure falls below ~25–30 psi, the fail-safe valve automatically shuts off all other gases (N2O, air) to prevent delivery of a hypoxic mixture.
⚠️ The fail-safe does NOT guarantee adequate oxygen supply — it only monitors pressure, not concentration.
Low O2 pressure alarm (audible) activates when O2 pipeline pressure falls below ~30 psi.
Modern machines include a minimum O2 ratio controller (Link-25 / Ratio-Master) that maintains at least 25% O2 in the fresh gas mixture.
⚠️ Critical: The fail-safe does NOT protect against crossed pipelines during hospital construction.
H-cylinders: Large free-standing cylinders. An H-cylinder of O2 contains ~6,900 liters at ~2200 psi.

topics.heading: Flowmeters (Rotameters)
bullets: Precision-calibrated, gas-specific glass or acrylic tubes containing a lightweight float (bobbin or ball).
Flow rate is read at the top of the float (ball) or midpoint of the bobbin.
On North American machines, OXYGEN is always on the RIGHT (closest to the common gas outlet) — prevents hypoxic mixtures in case of flowmeter tube cracks.
At low flows, the annular space is primarily determined by tube diameter (viscosity-dependent).
At high flows, float height is primarily determined by gas density.
Flowmeters are gas-specific and non-interchangeable.

rows: Reduces cylinder pressure to match pipeline

topics.heading: Oxygen Flush Valve & Vaporizers
bullets: Oxygen flush valve delivers 100% oxygen at 35–75 L/min directly to the common gas outlet, bypassing the flowmeters AND vaporizer.
⚠️ Cautions: (1) Barotrauma risk if used during inspiration; (2) Dilutes volatile agent — can cause awareness; (3) Valve sticking delivers continuous high O2 flow.
Modern vaporizers are variable-bypass, temperature-compensated, agent-specific (e.g., Datex-Ohmeda Tec 7, Draeger Vapor 2000).
⚡ KEY: Desflurane requires a SPECIAL electrically-heated, pressurized vaporizer (Tec 6) — boiling point 22.8°C is near room temperature; cannot use standard variable-bypass.
Vaporizers are interlocked — only one can be active at a time.
Tipping effect: Tilting a vaporizer can allow liquid anesthetic into the bypass chamber, causing a massive overdose. Transport upright.

rows: Standard variable-bypass; most common in USA

topics.heading: Anesthesia Machine Pre-Use Check (10-Step FDA)
bullets: 1. Auxiliary O2 supply (self-inflating bag/E-cylinder) available
2. Pipeline pressures adequate (~50 psi all gases)
3. E-cylinder backup pressure adequate (O2 >1000 psi)
4. Low-pressure circuit leak test (negative pressure or positive pressure test)
5. Flowmeter function and O2 ratio controller
6. Vaporizer fill level and no leaks
7. CO2 absorbent color and adequacy
8. Breathing circuit integrity (unidirectional valves, mask seal)
9. Scavenging system connected and functional
10. Monitors and alarms active and properly calibrated
⚡ KEY: Negative pressure (Madison) leak test checks the low-pressure circuit (flowmeters through vaporizer to common gas outlet). Must pass before every case.

topics.heading: Circle Breathing System
bullets: The most commonly used breathing circuit in the USA.
Allows rebreathing of exhaled gases after CO2 removal, conserving heat, moisture, and volatile agents.
Low-flow anesthesia (total FGF <1 L/min) is possible with the circle system due to CO2 absorption.
Risks at low flows: compound A accumulation (sevoflurane), CO production (desflurane/isoflurane + desiccated absorbent).

rows: Enters between absorber and inspiratory valve; delivers fresh O2/agent mix

Contains soda lime or Amsorb; removes CO2 from exhaled gas
Limits maximum circuit pressure; vents excess gas to scavenging

topics.heading: CO2 Absorbents
bullets: ⚡ KEY: Violet/purple color in soda lime = EXHAUSTED absorbent. Replace immediately. Color may partially revert to white after resting (regeneration) — this does NOT restore function.

⚡ KEY: Desiccated absorbent + desflurane or isoflurane → carbon monoxide (CO) production. More common on Monday mornings when machines have had high O2 flows all weekend. Turn off fresh gas flows when not in use.

topics.heading: Mapleson Circuits
bullets: Non-rebreathing (or minimal rebreathing) systems used for pediatric anesthesia, transport, and specific clinical situations.
⚡ KEY: Bain circuit check — before use, occlude the inner fresh gas tube while applying a low flow; if the flowmeter bobbin drops, the inner tube is intact (Pethick test).

topics.heading: Scavenging Systems (AGSS)
bullets: Anesthesia gas scavenging system (AGSS) captures waste anesthetic gases from the APL valve and ventilator relief valve, preventing OR pollution.
Chronic exposure linked to: spontaneous abortion, hepatotoxicity, and neurological effects in healthcare workers.
Components: gas-collecting assembly → transfer tubing → scavenging interface → disposal assembly (active vacuum or passive flow).
Interface contains pressure-relief valves to prevent both positive pressure (barotrauma) and negative pressure (lung collapse).
OSHA limits: trace N2O levels <25 ppm; trace halogenated agents <2 ppm (0.5 ppm when used with N2O).

topics.heading: Direct Laryngoscopy Blades
bullets: Direct laryngoscopy (DL) uses a rigid laryngoscope handle and blade to directly visualize the glottis.
Cormack-Lehane (C-L) grading: Grade I = full glottis; Grade II = posterior commissure only; Grade III = epiglottis only; Grade IV = no laryngeal structures.
⚡ KEY: BURP maneuver (Backward, Upward, Rightward Pressure on the thyroid cartilage) applied by an assistant can improve C-L grade during difficult laryngoscopy.

rows: Most common adult blade; wider flange displaces tongue easily
Pediatrics, anterior airways, long floppy epiglottis

topics.heading: Video Laryngoscopy
bullets: Video laryngoscopes (VL) use a camera mounted at the blade tip to project a magnified, indirect view onto a screen.
Improve laryngoscopic view by 1–2 grades vs. DL; invaluable for anticipated and unanticipated difficult airways.

⚡ KEY: An excellent VL view does NOT guarantee easy intubation. The hyperangulated blade requires a matching rigid stylet. Inability to navigate the ETT through the curve despite a great view is a recognized failure mode.
Indications: anticipated difficult airway, obesity, limited cervical spine mobility, limited mouth opening, previous difficult intubation, rescue after failed DL.

rows: Most widely studied VL; excellent view; requires stylet
Familiar Mac blade angle; easier to intubate once view obtained

Disposable; good for limited mouth opening

topics.heading: Flexible Fiberoptic Bronchoscope (FOB)
bullets: Transmits light and images via thousands of bundled optical fibers (fiberoptic) or via a CCD camera chip at the tip (videobronchoscope).
Intubating bronchoscopes have an outer diameter (OD) of 3.5–6.0 mm. ETT must have an ID at least 1 mm larger than the bronchoscope OD.
Most adult AFOI is performed with a 4.0–5.5 mm OD scope through a ≥6.0 mm ID ETT.

rows: Flexible shaft containing fiberoptic bundles, working channel, and control wires
Angulates up/down (180°/130° typical) via control lever

topics.heading: Awake Fiberoptic Intubation (AFOI)
bullets: ⚡ KEY: AFOI is the GOLD STANDARD technique for managing the anticipated difficult airway.
The patient is kept awake with topical anesthesia and light sedation while the scope is passed nasally or orally into the trachea, then the ETT is railroaded over the scope.

AFOI indications: anticipated difficult airway with full stomach, unstable C-spine, restricted mouth opening, large neck/mediastinal mass, airway pathology, or any situation where loss of airway could be catastrophic.
Topical anesthesia: Lidocaine 4% atomized to oropharynx, larynx, trachea; transtracheal block (2–3 mL lidocaine 4% through cricothyroid membrane).
Superior laryngeal nerve block (bilateral): 2–3 mL lidocaine 2% at superior cornu of thyroid cartilage.
Best sedation: Dexmedetomidine (sedation + mild analgesia without suppressing airway reflexes); midazolam (amnesia/anxiolysis); remifentanil (caution at higher doses).
Nasal AFOI: Decongest with oxymetazoline (Afrin), lubricate nasal passage, choose wider nostril.
Oral AFOI: Use a Berman or Ovassapian intubating airway to guide and protect the scope.

topics.heading: Standard ETT Sizing
bullets: ETTs are sized by internal diameter (ID) in millimeters.

⚡ KEY: Cuff pressure >30 cmH2O risks tracheal mucosal ischemia, necrosis, and post-extubation stenosis. Always check cuff pressure with a manometer — especially during N2O anesthesia (N2O diffuses into the cuff and increases pressure over time).
High-volume, low-pressure (HVLP) cuff: maintain at 20–30 cmH2O.

topics.heading: Double-Lumen Tubes (DLTs)
bullets: Most commonly used device for one-lung ventilation (OLV) in thoracic surgery.
Left-sided DLTs are safer (longer left mainstem bronchus); two lumens: one ending in trachea, one extending into left mainstem bronchus.
Sizing: Women <160 cm → 35Fr | Women >160 cm → 37Fr | Men <170 cm → 39Fr | Men >170 cm → 41Fr.
CT measurement of left mainstem bronchus diameter is the most accurate sizing method.
⚡ KEY: ALWAYS confirm DLT position with FOB after initial placement AND after patient repositioning (lateral decubitus position can cause DLT migration).
Via tracheal lumen: tracheal carina should be visible; blue bronchial cuff just below carina in left mainstem bronchus.
Via bronchial lumen: left upper lobe takeoff and left lower lobe bronchus should be visible.

topics.heading: SGA Overview & Generations
bullets: SGAs sit above the glottis, forming a low-pressure seal against the periglottic structures.
Used for: (1) routine airway management when ETT not required; (2) rescue devices in difficult/failed intubation; (3) conduits for fiberoptic intubation.

⚡ KEY — Contraindications to SGA use: full stomach (relative), pharyngeal pathology, restricted mouth opening <2.5 cm, morbid obesity (relative), prolonged prone positioning, airway pressures >20 cmH2O needed.

topics.heading: Cricothyrotomy Devices (eFONA)
bullets: Cricothyrotomy is the rescue technique for CICO (cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate) emergencies.
Access the airway through the cricothyroid membrane (CTM) — located between thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
⚡ KEY: The 'Scalpel-Bougie' technique is the recommended eFONA method (DAS 2015 guidelines): Stab → dilate (caudal traction on trachea) → insert bougie → railroad 6.0 ETT → inflate cuff → confirm.

topics.heading: Additional Intubation Accessories
bullets: HFNO / THRIVE: Heated, humidified oxygen at 30–70 L/min via nasal cannula. Creates apneic oxygenation via mass-flow effect and generates low PEEP. Extends safe apnea time up to 65+ minutes.
ETCO2 colorimetric detector: Disposable chemical detector that changes color in CO2; confirms tracheal intubation.
Esophageal detector device (EDD / bulb syringe): Esophagus collapses (no refill) = esophageal; trachea resists collapse (refills) = tracheal.
Tube exchanger (airway exchange catheter): Hollow, flexible catheter; can be left in trachea while ETT is changed over it.
HME (Heat and Moisture Exchanger): Passive humidifier/filter; conserves heat and moisture; placed between circuit Y-piece and ETT.

topics.heading: Electrical Safety in the OR
bullets: Line Isolation Monitor (LIM): The OR uses an isolated power system — neither conductor connected to ground. Prevents single-fault macroshock from flowing through a patient.
LIM alarms when isolation is compromised — identify and remove the faulty device. Procedure need not stop.
Macroshock: Current applied to the skin; requires >100 mA to cause VF; protected by skin resistance.
⚡ KEY — Microshock: Current applied directly to the heart (via pacing wires, intracardiac catheters); as little as 10 µA can cause VF. Patient is 10,000× more sensitive.
⚡ KEY: Any patient with an intracardiac catheter (pacemaker wire, PA catheter) is at risk for microshock. All equipment near such patients must be grounded and in good repair.

topics.heading: Spinal & Epidural Needles
bullets: ⚡ KEY — PDPH: Positional headache (worse upright, better supine) due to CSF leak through dural hole. Risk factors: larger needle, cutting vs. pencil-point tip, female sex, young age.
PDPH treatment: bed rest, hydration, caffeine, and epidural blood patch (gold standard) — 15–20 mL autologous blood into epidural space.

rows: Traditional spinal; fast CSF flow; good for diagnostic LP

topics.heading: Ultrasound-Guided Regional Anesthesia
bullets: Ultrasound guidance (USG) enables real-time visualization of nerves, adjacent structures, and needle tip position while observing local anesthetic spread.
Reduces: block failure rates, LA doses required, and complication rates (vascular puncture, pneumothorax).
Nerve stimulator: Delivers controlled electrical current (0.5 mA, 0.1 ms) through an insulated needle tip. Motor response at <0.5 mA confirms needle proximity to nerve.
⚠️ Current <0.2 mA with motor response may indicate intraneural placement — STOP and reposition.

topics.heading: IV Catheter Sizes & Flow Rates
bullets: ⚡ KEY: Flow rate is inversely proportional to catheter length and directly proportional to the 4th power of the radius (Poiseuille's Law). A short, large-bore catheter (14–16G) provides dramatically higher flow than a long central line for rapid resuscitation.

topics.heading: Central Venous Catheters & Arterial Lines
bullets: CVCs are placed in large central veins (IJ, subclavian, femoral) for CVP monitoring, drug delivery (vasopressors, TPN, vesicants).
Complications of CVC: arterial puncture, pneumothorax (highest risk with subclavian), air embolism, catheter malposition, CLABSI, thrombosis, nerve injury.
Arterial lines: radial artery (most common — perform Allen's test first), femoral, brachial, or dorsalis pedis.

⚡ KEY — Phlebostatic axis: Reference point for zeroing all hemodynamic pressure transducers. Located at the intersection of the 4th intercostal space and the mid-axillary line — approximates the level of the right atrium.

sections.heading: Study Strategy
bullets: Step 1 — Benchmark: Take the full 100-question practice test cold to identify your weakest domain before studying.
Step 2 — Study by domain: Spend the most time on General Principles of Anesthesia (35%), the largest domain.
Step 3 — Active recall: After each section, close the guide and write down everything you remember.
Step 4 — Re-test: Re-do practice questions for any domain scoring below 70%.
Step 5 — Final review: In the 48 hours before the exam, review only High-Yield boxes and Clinical Pearls.

Scoring: Scaled score 0-900; passing standard 450 (adjusting July 1, 2026).

bullets: Frank-Starling law: increased preload → increased stroke volume (to a point)

Alveolar gas equation: PAO₂ = (FiO₂)(PB - PH₂O) - PaCO₂/0.8

sections.heading: Applied Physics
bullets: Boyle's Law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ — pressure/volume inversely proportional (compressed gas cylinders)
Henry's Law: Gas solubility proportional to partial pressure — basis for blood:gas partition coefficients
Graham's Law: Diffusion rate inversely proportional to √molecular weight — CO₂ diffuses faster than O₂
Laplace's Law: T = P × r / 2w — smaller alveoli tend to collapse; countered by surfactant
Poiseuille's Law: Flow = (Pr⁴π)/(8ηl) — doubling tube radius increases flow 16×
Fick Principle: CO = O₂ consumption / (CaO₂ - CvO₂); normal SvO₂ 75%
ABL = EBV × (Hi - Hf) / Hi; EBV = 65-70 mL/kg adult

sections.heading: Equipment Troubleshooting
bullets: High peak pressure + normal plateau: airway obstruction (bronchospasm, ETT kink, secretions)
High peak AND plateau: decreased compliance (pneumothorax, endobronchial intubation, ARDS)
Sudden ETCO₂ drop to zero: esophageal intubation, circuit disconnect, cardiac arrest
Gradual ETCO₂ decline: pulmonary embolism, decreased CO, hyperventilation
O₂ E-tank: full ~2000 psig; duration = remaining psig × 0.3 / FGF rate

value.title: Domain III: General Principles of Anesthesia (35%)

rows: Well-controlled DM, HTN, BMI 30-40, smoker, pregnancy
Poorly controlled DM/HTN, COPD, morbid obesity, ESRD, CVA history
Recent MI (<3 mo), sepsis, DIC, severe valve disease
Ruptured AAA, massive trauma, intracranial bleed
Clear liquids (water, juice without pulp, black coffee, tea)

sections.heading: Preoperative Medications
bullets: Beta-blockers: Continue perioperatively; initiating new BB day of surgery increases stroke risk
ACE inhibitors/ARBs: Hold morning of surgery — refractory intraoperative hypotension risk
Clopidogrel: Hold 5-7 days before elective surgery with neuraxial
Herbal supplements: Garlic/ginkgo (bleeding), ginseng (hypoglycemia), St. John's Wort (drug interactions), kava (sedation)

sections.heading: Difficult Airway — LEMON Assessment
bullets: L — Look: Facial trauma, obesity, micrognathia, retrognathia, large incisors
E — Evaluate 3-3-2 rule: Mouth >3 fingers, hyoid-chin >3 fingers, hyoid-thyroid notch >2 fingers
M — Mallampati: Score I-IV; III-IV associated with difficult intubation
O — Obstruction: Stridor, foreign body, abscess, angioedema, tumor
N — Neck mobility: Cervical disease, obesity; reduced extension = difficult laryngoscopy

sections.heading: ASA Difficult Airway Algorithm
bullets: Awake intubation: preferred when difficult airway anticipated AND patient cannot tolerate apnea safely
Awake fiberoptic: gold standard; topicalize with nebulized lidocaine + superior laryngeal nerve block
RSI: succinylcholine 1.5-2 mg/kg OR rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg + sugammadex available
CICO: declare emergency → supraglottic device → cricothyrotomy if SGA fails
Extubation of difficult airway: airway exchange catheter; extubate fully awake

sections.heading: Neuraxial Complications
bullets: High spinal (above T4): hypotension, bradycardia, loss of intercostal breathing; C3-C5 = phrenic paralysis → intubate
PDPH: positional headache; blood patch (15-20 mL) is definitive treatment; onset 24-48h post dural puncture
Peripheral blocks: TAP (T10-L1), femoral/adductor (knee), popliteal sciatic (foot), paravertebral (thorax/breast)

rows: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with large volumes; use in head trauma, hyperkalemia
Most physiologic; preferred for most surgical cases
Most balanced pH; no calcium; large volume resuscitation
Volume expansion; useful in hepatic failure; no mortality benefit over crystalloid
Transfuse at Hgb <7 g/dL; 1 unit raises Hgb ~1 g/dL
<50,000 for surgery; <100,000 for neurosurgery; <10,000 for prophylaxis

sections.heading: Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP)
bullets: 1:1:1 ratio — PRBC:FFP:Platelets
Add cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen <150 mg/dL (<200 in OB hemorrhage)
TXA 1g IV within 3 hours of traumatic hemorrhage — significantly reduces mortality
Monitor with TEG/ROTEM for goal-directed transfusion

Cerebral edema, brachial plexus stretch, ETT migration caudad
Peroneal nerve palsy (most common), compartment syndrome if >4h
Axillary roll required (NOT in axilla); down lung atelectasis
ETT dislodgement on turning, corneal abrasion, facial edema
VAE risk highest; paradoxical air embolism if PFO
High-pitched stridor, paradoxical chest, SpO₂ drop
Jaw thrust, 100% O₂, CPAP; succinylcholine 0.1-0.5 mg/kg
CPAP/BiPAP, diuresis; occurs after forceful inspiration against closed glottis
Weak grip, head lift <5 sec, paradoxical breathing
Verify TOF >0.9 before extubation; sugammadex or neostigmine
Apfel score; ondansetron, dexamethasone, scopolamine; TIVA reduces PONV
Meperidine 25 mg IV most effective; warming; clonidine

value.title: Domain IV: Anesthesia for Surgical Procedures & Special Populations (25%)

rows: CPB: heparin 300-400 units/kg, ACT >400 sec; cardioplegia; protamine reversal; TEE essential
ICP: head up 15-30°, avoid N₂O, mannitol 0.25-1 g/kg, avoid ketamine; TIVA for neuromonitoring
OLV: DLT or bronchial blocker; TV 4-6 mL/kg IBW; CPAP nondependent lung for refractory hypoxia
CO₂ pneumoperitoneum: increased PaCO₂, ICP, airway pressure; watch for CO₂ embolism
Fat embolism with IM reaming; tourniquet deflation: hypotension/metabolic acidosis; regional preferred
Oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia with EOM traction) → atropine; avoid succinylcholine in open globe

sections.heading: Venous Air Embolism (VAE)
bullets: Highest risk: sitting/beach chair craniotomy, posterior fossa, hepatic resection, spine surgery
Signs: mill-wheel murmur, decreased ETCO₂, increased ETN₂, hypotension, dysrhythmias
TEE is most sensitive; Doppler most practical
Treatment: flood field, Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus + Trendelenburg), 100% O₂, D/C N₂O, aspirate through CVP catheter

sections.heading: Pediatric Anesthesia
bullets: Airway: obligate nasal breathers <6 mo; narrowest at cricoid (not glottis) until ~8 years; large tongue, omega epiglottis
ETT size (uncuffed): (Age/4) + 4; ETT depth (cm at lip): weight (kg) + 10 or age/2 + 12
Inhalation induction: sevoflurane with 70% N₂O; MAC higher in infants (sevoflurane MAC 3.3% neonates)
Fluid maintenance: 4/2/1 rule (4 mL/kg/h × first 10 kg; 2 × next 10 kg; 1 × each kg >20)
Laryngospasm: 0.87% incidence vs. 0.08% adults — most common peds anesthesia complication

rows: Pre-oxygenate 3-5 min; early desaturation during intubation
Delayed gastric emptying; decreased LES tone
RSI for all GA after 12-18 weeks gestation

sections.heading: Obstetric Key Points
bullets: Cesarean spinal: Hyperbaric bupivacaine 10-12 mg + fentanyl 15-25 mcg + preservative-free morphine 0.1-0.2 mg; target T4
Spinal hypotension: Phenylephrine first-line (preserves uteroplacental blood flow better than ephedrine)
HELLP: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets; platelet threshold for epidural >75,000-80,000
PPH: Oxytocin first-line (20-40 units/L LR); if refractory: methylergonovine, 15-methyl-PGF2α, misoprostol
Amniotic fluid embolism: Sudden CV collapse + DIC + hypoxia; supportive; highly lethal

sections.heading: Geriatric Anesthesia
bullets: Pharmacokinetics: Decreased hepatic/renal function → prolonged drug effect; decreased albumin → more free drug
MAC decreases ~6% per decade after age 40
Closing capacity exceeds FRC at ~age 65 supine → increased V/Q mismatch
POCD risk increases with age, depth, duration, polypharmacy; avoid benzodiazepines

sections.heading: Anesthesia for Obesity
bullets: Airway: ramped position (ear to sternal notch); 25° head-up reduces aspiration risk; preoxygenate optimally
Dosing: IBW for volatile MAC; LBW for most IV drugs; TBW for succinylcholine
Screen for OSA: STOP-BANG ≥3 = high risk (Snoring, Tired, Observed apnea, Pressure/HTN, BMI>35, Age>50, Neck>40cm, Male)
Bariatric surgery: RSI required; minimize opioids post-op in OSA patients

sections.heading: MUDPILES — High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis

rows: Visual symptoms with methanol; lactic acidosis with metformin
Renal failure — accumulation of organic acids
Shock, sepsis, ischemia, cyanide, liver failure
Antifreeze; calcium oxalate crystals in urine

sections.heading: Cardiac Dysrhythmias — Perioperative Management
bullets: SVT: Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push (12 mg ×2 if needed); cardiovert if unstable
A-fib with RVR: Rate control (metoprolol, diltiazem); cardiovert if hemodynamically unstable
VT (pulseless): Defibrillate 200J biphasic; amiodarone 300 mg IV; follow ACLS
VF: Immediate defibrillation; CPR; epinephrine 1 mg q3-5 min
Bradycardia: Atropine 0.5 mg IV (up to 3 mg); pacing if refractory
Torsades: Magnesium sulfate 1-2 g IV; correct QT-prolonging drugs

sections.heading: 5 Hs and 5 Ts — Reversible Causes of Cardiac Arrest
bullets: 5 Hs: Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion (acidosis), Hypo/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia
5 Ts: Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Toxins, Thrombosis (pulmonary), Thrombosis (coronary)
Treat all reversible causes simultaneously during CPR
TEE is invaluable in unexplained intraoperative cardiac arrest

sections.heading: Final Board Day Checklist
bullets: 4 domains: Basic Sciences 20%, Equipment 20%, General Principles 35%, Surgical/Special 25%
The NCE is adaptive — a hard question is a GOOD sign; stay calm and keep going
For MCR "select ALL that apply": evaluate each option independently; no partial credit
If exam stops at 100 questions — do NOT assume you failed; most passes occur at minimum count
Pass rate (2025): 90.5% first-time — the odds are strongly in your favor
